records.t: The folder holds 5 reference documents, and 14 of the rules that decide a tender are printed in them
records.s: These are the only statements of procedure in the archive. Everything quoted here is from a PDF in the folder, named with its page. The standard tender document among them is marked on its own first page as a preliminary working draft, and no notice in this archive names the standard document it was written from, so these rules describe the procedure as the supplied copies state it rather than the

records.t: Both printed tests of whether a price is reasonable need something this archive never prints
records.s: The low-price test is run on the prices of the technically responsive tenderers, and the clause says how many it takes: "(at least two tenders)". It weighs those prices against an official cost estimate (2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p30; the sentence on that page is broken by the clause heading printed in the margin). The other test rejects a tender whose evaluated price deviates from that same

records.t: Nothing in the folder sets a minimum number of tenderers for an open tender
records.s: A sweep of all 231 reference pages for any phrase that puts a floor under a count of tenders or tenderers returns 1: "at least two tenders", which is the condition on the low-price test rather than a condition on holding the tender. Weak competition appears once as a ground on which a procuring entity *may* end a tender - "there is evidence of lack of effective competition; such as non-participati

records.t: The typical tender in this archive was open for 22 days, the shortest for 8 and the longest for 97, and every one of the 1129 that printed both dates was opened on the day it closed
records.s: The window is counted from the date the notice says it was published to the date it says tendering closed. Half the archive falls between 16 and 28 days. The tenders were opened the same day they closed in every case, which is what an electronic system does automatically, and the last day a tender document could be bought was a median of one day before closing. Works packages stayed open slightly

records.t: One rule in the folder can be re-run against the notices from end to end, and it holds in every case: the tender security must stay valid at least 28 days past the tender's own expiry, and all 1118 notices that print both dates do - 1110 of them by exactly 28 days
records.s: The rule is printed at 2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p23: the security shall "remain valid for at least twenty-eight (28) days beyond the expiry date of the Tender Validity in order to make a claim in due course against a T". Both dates it needs are on the face of the notice, so this is the only test on this site where the record answers the rule without anything having to be assumed. Nothing fal

records.t: The folder calls a tender validity period of 60 to 150 days normal; 0 of the 1102 notices that print it fall below 60, and 17 run to 180 days
records.s: The same page of the standard tender document that sets the band also says a shorter or longer period "may be authorized by HOPE or Authorized Officer" (2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p39), so a period outside the band is something the rule provides for rather than something it forbids. Four lengths account for almost the whole archive - 120 days in 603 notices, 90 days in 435 notices, 60 days in

records.t: Nothing in the folder says how long a national tender must stay open, and all 1150 of these tenders are national
records.s: Every notice in the archive prints its procurement type as NCT - national competitive tendering. The folder prints exactly two figures for how long bidders must be given, both on one page of chapter2_en.pdf: "not less than 45 days shall be allowed for international bidding." and "not less than 90 days shall be allowed to enable prospective bidders to conduct investigations at the site before submi

records.t: 160 of the 1150 tender notices carry an amendment, 144 of them printing a table of what changed; of the 735 changes those tables list, 216 print an old value and a new value that are the same
records.s: The amendment is printed on the notice itself, so a notice downloaded today shows the amended values and not the ones first advertised. The change table is the only place in the archive where both versions appear. Where a row lists a field but prints the same value twice, the document does not say what about that field changed, and this analysis does not guess: the row is counted as listed and not

records.t: All 404 date changes the amendment tables print move the date later; none moves it earlier. The 104 changes to a closing date, across 88 tenders, add a median of 7.0 days each
records.s: An extension gives everyone who is still watching more time, and the direction is the same in every case the archive prints: not one deadline in the amendment tables was brought forward. The documents do not print who asked for the extension, except in the few notices quoted under F-AMEND-05.

records.t: For the 83 amended tenders where both versions can be dated, the bidding window as first advertised was a median of 22 days and the window after amendment a median of 30 days - so the 22-day median this investigation reports for the whole archive is the amended figure, not the one bidders first saw
records.s: The closing date in the dataset is the one the notice prints today, which for an amended tender is the extended one. That matters for reading the clock: a short window that was later extended is recorded here at its extended length, so the count of short windows is a floor and not a ceiling. It cannot be corrected in the other direction, because a tender whose window was shortened would show the s

records.t: In 36 tenders the requirement to enter was rewritten after the notice was published. The change tables print 10 money thresholds in both versions; 7 of them move in a direction that can be read, 6 down and 1 up
records.s: This is the one place in the archive where a rule of entry can be read in both versions, so it is the one place where the direction of a change is a matter of record rather than inference. Most of the movement is downward, and the largest of it is a factor of 5.0: tender 100483 cut the turnover a bidder had to show from 20.00 Corers to 4.00 Corers. The 1 that went the other way is tender 174037, w

records.t: No amendment in the archive prints the date it was made, and only 16 of the 160 amendment notices print any ground for the change; so whether a rule was rewritten before or after firms bought the tender document cannot be established from these documents
records.s: The amendment carries a number - first, second - and a free-text note that is usually a description of the field that moved rather than a reason for moving it. The only place in the whole archive where an amendment date is even provided for is a blank in BPPA's own standard document, which reads "Amendment is [insert effective date] or upon execution whichever is later". The notices as published l

records.t: 545 of the 1150 tender notices print at least one rule of entry a reader can check; 615 print at least one clause that points at a document the portal does not publish, and 10 do both
records.s: Every notice in this archive prints an "Eligibility of Tenderer" heading, so nothing is missing from the page. What differs is what follows the heading. 615 clauses across 615 notices say only that the criteria are as per the Tender Data Sheet, the Instructions to Tenderers or the tender document - documents obtainable by buying the tender document, and not among the 1,805 PDFs. For the 605 notice

records.t: Of the 3239 clauses the notices print, 1327 read as ordinary for this archive, 870 set themselves apart in one way, 59 name a particular product, and 22 do two or more of those at once
records.s: The labels are defined by the arithmetic printed beside them and carry no finding about anyone's conduct. "Ordinary for this archive" means only that other notices in this same archive ask for the same thing; it is not a statement about what procurement elsewhere asks for. The remaining 961 clauses state no rule that can be measured here.

records.t: Across the 591 award notices that print bid counts, 3436 documents were sold, 2749 bids arrived, 1752 were found responsive and 591 contracts were signed
records.s: Every figure is the sum of a number printed on the award notice itself. The four stages are not four measurements of the same thing: a document may be bought and never used, and a bid may arrive and be set aside before it is evaluated.

records.t: No supplied document names a single bidder, a single price or a single reason for rejection
records.s: The 2749 bids that arrived and the 1752 found responsive are counts only. There is no bidder list, no quoted price, no evaluated amount, no ranking, no score and no per-bidder reason in any of the 1,805 PDFs. Anything about who lost, or why, is outside what these documents can establish.

records.t: 201 of 591 tenders reached the award stage with exactly one responsive bid (34.0%)
records.s: A single responsive bid is not in itself irregular - a tender can draw one serious bidder. It does mean the price was not compared with any other price at the moment of award, and in 87 of these the notice records only one bid arriving at all.

records.t: In 256 tenders every bid that arrived was found responsive; in 335 at least one was set aside
records.s: The number set aside per tender runs from 0 to 54. The documents print the count and never the ground, so each of these is a question for the procuring entity, not an answer.

records.t: Sorting the 591 tenders that printed their counts by the strongest clause each one printed does not separate them: the share ending with a single responsive tenderer is 48.0% where a clause matched two or more of the tests and 33.4% everywhere else, a difference this many tenders would produce by chance about 14 times in a hundred
records.s: This is the join the investigation exists to test, and it comes back empty. Only 25 of the 591 tenders with printed counts carry a clause labelled RESTRICTIVE-LOOKING PATTERN or HIGHLY SPECIFIC, so the comparison is between a small group and a large one and only a large difference could be read as anything; the two-sided Fisher exact p is 0.137 for ending with one responsive tenderer and 0.683 for

records.t: The folder recommends that the cash a tenderer must hold be 80 to 100 percent of the estimated cost, and 60 to 80 percent for the past contract it must show; measured against the contract value actually signed, the middle of this archive sits at 75 and 70 percent, and 25.5% and 29.2% of tenders sit above the band
records.s: Both bands are printed on one page of the standard tender document in the folder (2026-01-04-13-47-03-e-PG3A.pdf p38) and both are advisory: the word is recommended, and the first page of that document calls itself a preliminary working draft. Both measure against the estimated cost of the procurement, and no notice or award in this archive prints an estimated cost, so the comparison here is again

records.t: 20 clauses in 17 notices print a sum of money that cannot be read off the page with certainty, and they are left unread rather than guessed at
records.s: A figure in a Bangladeshi tender notice is usually printed twice, once in digits and once in words - "Tk 1.20 [One point Two] Crore" - and the words are what make the digits legible, because the scale word can belong to the digits or stand apart from them. Where the two contradict each other, or where the scale word beside the figure is one letter from a real one and so does not settle which was m

records.t: Of the 1150 tender notices, 700 say a contract was awarded, 135 were re-tendered or are to be, 46 were rejected, 26 cancelled and 183 print no outcome at all
records.s: The status is a field on the notice, printed by the portal. It is the only account of the ending that most of these tenders have: 641 of the 700 that say a contract was awarded have an award notice in this archive, and 59 do not, so for those the winner, the value and the bid counts are not on the record here. In the other direction 1 award notice names a tender whose own notice is not in the arch

records.t: 207 tenders ended without a contract and not one of them prints why
records.s: The portal prints an ending - re-tendered, to be re-tendered, rejected, cancelled - and stops. No document in the archive gives a ground for any of them: not a tender that drew no responsive bid, not one annulled for weak competition, not one rejected because every price was too far from an estimate. The folder's own rules name those as things that can happen (R-ANNUL-COMPETITION, R-ALL-NON, R-EST

records.t: 309 firms are named as winners across 645 award notices worth 3723.68 crore taka, and 9 of them - 2.9% - account for half of it
records.s: Every figure is the sum of contract values printed on award notices. The largest single share belongs to Spectra Engineers Ltd.: 1067.95 crore taka across 4 contracts, 28.7% of all the money in this archive. 105 firms won more than one contract and 204 won exactly one. The most frequent winner by count is M/S. A. R. Enterprise with 15 contracts worth 19.24 crore taka. A concentrated distribution i

records.t: 68 of the 309 winning firms won from more than one procuring entity, and one won from 7
records.s: A firm winning from several offices is ordinary in itself. It is recorded here because it is the only cross-office trace the archive supports: Momotaj Engineers Ltd. won 10 contracts across 7 procuring entities in Dhaka. Whether the same firms competed against each other in those tenders cannot be answered, because no notice names a bidder who did not win.

records.t: 34 of the 309 winning firms declare who owns them, and no person named in those declarations is declared an owner of more than one of them
records.s: The archive carries 77 ownership declarations naming 49 people. 58 of them print no designation and 45 print no country. For the other 275 firms - 89.0% of the winners - the award notice names the company and stops, so who stands behind it is not on the public record. The question this investigation would most want to ask of a procurement archive is whether the same people own firms that win from

records.t: 10 printed addresses in the archive are shared by more than one named firm; 8 of the 10 involve a joint venture printed at its partner's address
records.s: An address is printed on the award notice, so this is the government's own record of where a winner sits. Most of these read plainly: a joint venture is registered at the address of one of the firms inside it, and the notice names the partners in the same string. The 2 that do not involve a joint venture are the ones worth a second look, because in each the two firms are also near-identical in nam

records.t: 219 pairs of names in this archive resemble each other closely enough to be worth checking, and 0 were merged
records.s: Two names that look alike are not one entity. 55 pairs differ by at most two characters - "Aliza Enterprise" against "M/S. Maliha Enterprise" is one of them - and 164 have one name's words entirely inside the other, which is what a joint venture's name does to its partner's. Merging either kind on sight would silently rewrite who won what, so every pair is recorded with its measure and none is mer

The count is not a score and does not rank anyone: the observations overlap heavily - a tender with one responsive bid has usually also set bids aside - and no supplied document finds that any of them was improper. how_to_read: one record per thing a reader might look for. k is the kind, t the name, s the line under it, f the values a scoped query matches (company:, person:, agency:, tender:, district:, status:, label:, file: and the rest of scopes), n the numbers a range query compares (amount:a..b, year:a..b), d the dates (date:a..b), and r the file and page it was printed on. Values in f, and r.file, are indexes into strings. The words that are searchable but not displayed are in text.json, one entry per record id, fetched only when a query needs a phrase checked. Document text is not here; it is in investigation/public/pages/.
